Managing with AI - Organizational Synthesis
Page 1
 TASK 3 - SYNTHESIS DIVERGENCE
 Deep contrast of the key approaches identified in the topographical mapping
Objective. Task 3 examines the main tensions identified in Task 2. Rather than selecting a single superior scheduling
technology, it contrasts alternative knowledge streams to expose the trade-offs the organization must manage when
introducing intelligent automation into steel and furnace operations.
Three divergences are especially relevant because they connect the technical core of the Document Set with the
structural gap identified in the cross-reference network.

Evidence from the Document Set. D05 applies a two-stage DRL framework to energy optimization in a steel
enterprise under supply and demand uncertainty, illustrating the adaptive potential of learning-based decision-making.
D21 similarly uses multi-agent reinforcement learning to coordinate production scheduling and energy management. In
contrast, D22 and D29 demonstrate the continuing value of explicit mathematical and robust optimization for
energy-aware and uncertainty-aware steel scheduling.
 TRADE-OFF: Model transparency and explicit constraint control <-> Adaptability and learning
 capability
Organizational implication. The choice should not be framed as optimization or AI. Model-based optimization offers a
strong representation of feasibility, while DRL offers adaptive capabilities. A hybrid architecture can use explicit
constraints to define safe feasible decisions while learning-based methods improve responsiveness.

Evidence from the Document Set. D10 uses a Digital Twin for scheduling walking-beam reheating furnaces, linking
the optimization problem with the actual state of the physical process. D26 and D31 similarly connect Digital Twins and
live production information with adaptive scheduling. D18 and D24 reinforce the need for real-time or rolling-horizon
responses to disturbances and uncertainty.
 TRADE-OFF: Optimization simplicity <-> Real-world fidelity and adaptability
Organizational implication. Increasing algorithmic sophistication is insufficient if the scheduling model is disconnected
from the physical plant. Real-time adaptation requires a reliable information layer capable of representing current
equipment, furnace, product and energy conditions.

Evidence from the Document Set. D04 and D06 explicitly address the transparency and explainability problem in
AI-supported planning and scheduling. D13 links multi-agent DRL with XAI in production control, while D16 introduces
human feedback into dynamic scheduling. D25 extends the issue to high-stakes process industries, emphasizing
human involvement and safe deployment.
 TRADE-OFF: Automation autonomy and algorithmic complexity <-> Explainability, human control and
 safe deployment
Organizational implication. In a high-stakes industrial environment, optimization performance alone is insufficient. The
organization must decide which actions can be automated, which require explanations, and which should remain
subject to human review or escalation.

Conclusion. The divergence analysis shows that the organizational challenge cannot be solved by maximizing a single
technological capability. Traditional optimization provides explicit constraints but may struggle with highly dynamic
environments; learning-based approaches increase adaptability but introduce data, validation and interpretability
challenges; Digital Twins improve real-world fidelity but require greater infrastructure and integration; and increasing
automation creates a stronger need for explainability and human oversight. The central challenge is therefore to
manage these trade-offs rather than selecting one approach in isolation.

 TASK 4 - INTEGRATIVE SYNTHESIS
 Organizational blueprint for intelligent, energy-efficient and human-supervised steel scheduling
Objective. Task 4 re-converges the tensions identified in Task 3 into one implementable organizational blueprint. The
proposed architecture combines the complementary strengths of Digital Twins (DTs), Deep Reinforcement Learning
(DRL), mathematical optimization, Explainable AI (XAI), metallurgical constraints and human oversight.

4.3 Role of the Key Technologies
Digital Twin - Know what is happening. The Digital Twin acts as the bridge between the physical plant and the
decision system. It updates the representation of furnaces, products and production resources so that scheduling
decisions reflect actual operating conditions. This role is strongly represented by D10, D26 and D31.
DRL and Intelligent Optimization - Decide what to do. DRL and related learning-based methods provide adaptive
decision-making when production and energy conditions change. They should complement, rather than blindly replace,
model-based optimization where hard constraints must be guaranteed. D05 and D21 illustrate this adaptive
energy/production decision-making role.
Metallurgical Constraints - Ensure feasibility. Physical and operational rules define the feasible decision space.
AI-generated schedules remain subordinate to furnace capacity, thermal requirements, sequencing/interlock rules,
process routes and equipment availability. The furnace-specific studies, particularly D10, D22 and D23, demonstrate
why these constraints cannot be abstracted away.
XAI - Explain why. XAI provides traceability and understandable reasons for complex scheduling recommendations,
supporting operator trust and review. D04, D06, D08 and D13 form the main explainability stream in the Document Set.
Human Oversight - Govern execution. Human supervision provides the final governance layer. Routine validated
decisions can operate with human-on-the-loop monitoring, while novel, uncertain or safety-critical cases should trigger
human review or escalation. D16 and D25 are particularly relevant to this deployment layer.

4.5 Implementation Principles
1. Use the Digital Twin as the real-time information layer, keeping the scheduling model aligned with actual production
conditions.

2. Preserve metallurgical and operational constraints as hard boundaries for feasible AI decisions.
3. Combine mathematical optimization with DRL/AI rather than treating them as mutually exclusive alternatives.
4. Integrate XAI into the decision interface so operators can understand why schedules change and which trade-offs are
being made.
5. Apply risk-based human oversight, increasing human authority as uncertainty, novelty or safety criticality increases.
4.6 Final Integrative Synthesis
Integrative Synthesis. The Document Set does not support a purely algorithmic view of intelligent steel scheduling.
Instead, the synthesis suggests a hybrid, closed-loop organizational architecture in which Digital Twins provide real-time
visibility of the physical plant; metallurgical and operational constraints define the feasible decision space; mathematical
optimization and DRL provide complementary optimization and adaptive capabilities; XAI translates complex
recommendations into understandable information; and human oversight governs their safe execution.
The resulting system should therefore be understood not as autonomous AI replacing the production scheduler, but as
an adaptive decision-support and automation architecture in which the level of autonomy depends on operational
uncertainty and decision criticality. This integration directly addresses the principal divergence identified in Task 3:
achieving the adaptability and performance benefits of intelligent automation without disconnecting decisions from
physical feasibility, human understanding and industrial safety.
